everyday-description: Never touched crypto? Start here. Every lesson begins with something you already know, like a notebook, a mailbox or a vending machine.
everyday-notebook-summary: Why a notebook with thousands of copies is hard to cheat.
everyday-notebook-picture-p1: Imagine a notebook that thousands of people keep identical copies of. A new line goes into every copy, but if someone changes an old line in theirs, the other copies still show the real one.
everyday-notebook-try-prompt: Add a new line to the notebook. Then change an old line in your copy and see what the other copies do.
everyday-notebook-try-explain: The new line reached every copy. Your change stayed in your copy alone, so the others still show the real line and ignore yours.
everyday-notebook-reveal-p1: No single copy is in charge. Every copy checks each new line, and the version they agree on is the real one.
everyday-notebook-reveal-p2: Ethereum works like that notebook, shared by computers all over the world. Its notebook is called a blockchain.
everyday-notebook-change-prompt: Someone changes an old line in their copy of Ethereum's blockchain to give themselves extra money. What happens?
everyday-notebook-change-opt-counts: The change counts, because it's in their copy
everyday-notebook-change-fb-counts: Only their own copy says so. Think about what all the other copies show.
everyday-notebook-change-opt-ignored: Nothing: the other copies still show the real line
everyday-notebook-change-fb-ignored: Right. Every other copy still has the real line, so a secret change gets nowhere.
everyday-notebook-change-opt-copied: Every other copy updates to match
everyday-notebook-change-fb-copied: Copies don't simply take on each other's edits. Think about what the other copies still show.
everyday-notebook-takeaway-p1: A blockchain is like a notebook that computers all over the world keep identical copies of, so nobody can secretly change it.
everyday-cash-summary: Ethereum's own money, and sending it without a bank.
everyday-cash-picture-p1: Hand a friend cash, and it goes straight from you to them. Pay by bank transfer, and you ask your bank to move it for you.
everyday-cash-try-prompt: It's late at night and your bank's app is down. Your friend is right next to you, and you owe them for dinner. How can you pay them back now?
everyday-cash-try-fb-cash: Right. Cash doesn't need anyone's permission or opening hours. It goes straight from you to your friend.
everyday-cash-try-fb-transfer: With the app down, the transfer has to wait for the bank. Think about a way that skips the bank.
everyday-cash-try-opt-wait: You can't until the bank is back
everyday-cash-try-fb-wait: One way of paying doesn't involve a bank at all.
everyday-cash-reveal-p1: Ethereum has its own money, called ETH. Sending it works like handing over cash: no bank in the middle, just a new line on the blockchain.
everyday-cash-approve-prompt: You send ETH to a friend in another country at midnight. Does a bank have to approve it before it goes through?
everyday-cash-approve-opt-bank: Yes, your bank, once it opens
everyday-cash-approve-fb-bank: ETH doesn't move through your bank. Think about how cash changes hands.
everyday-cash-approve-opt-both: Yes, a bank in each country
everyday-cash-approve-fb-both: Borders don't matter here: there's one blockchain for the whole world. Think about how cash changes hands.
everyday-cash-approve-opt-none: No: no bank is involved at all
everyday-cash-approve-fb-none: Right. Like cash, ETH needs no bank's permission, at any hour. The computers keeping the blockchain check it and add it as a new line.
everyday-cash-takeaway-p1: ETH is Ethereum's own money. Like cash, it goes straight from you to someone else, with no bank in the middle.
everyday-mailbox-summary: Where people send you ETH, and the key that lets you spend it.
everyday-mailbox-picture-p1: Picture a mailbox with a glass door. Anyone can drop money through the slot and see what's inside, but only your key opens the door to take it out.
everyday-mailbox-try-prompt: This is your mailbox. Drag or tap each payment into the slot, then try every key in the lock.
everyday-mailbox-try-explain: Anyone could drop money in, and anyone can see it through the glass, but only your own key opened the door.
everyday-mailbox-reveal-p1: In Ethereum, your mailbox is an address: anyone can send ETH to it and see what it holds. Its key is your private key, the only way to spend that ETH.
everyday-mailbox-reveal-p2: A wallet is an app that keeps your key. Your ETH stays at your address on the blockchain.
everyday-mailbox-phone-prompt: Losing your key doesn't empty your mailbox. So if the phone with your wallet app breaks, where is your ETH?
everyday-mailbox-phone-fb-gone: The phone only held your key. Think about where your mailbox is.
everyday-mailbox-phone-opt-maker: With the company that made the wallet app
everyday-mailbox-phone-fb-maker: This app only kept your key. The company that made it never had your ETH.
everyday-mailbox-phone-opt-address: Still at your address on the blockchain
everyday-mailbox-phone-fb-address: Right. Your ETH never left your address. But to reach it again you need a backup of your key, so always make one. A later lesson shows how.
everyday-mailbox-takeaway-p1: Your address is a glass mailbox anyone can send ETH to and see into. Your private key is the only way to spend it, and your wallet keeps that key, not your ETH.
everyday-stamp-summary: Why every payment carries a small fee, and why its price changes.
everyday-stamp-picture-p1: Every letter needs a stamp to pay for its delivery, and heavier mail needs more stamps. Without them, the post office would be buried in junk mail.
everyday-stamp-try-prompt: You're mailing a heavy box of books instead of a letter. What does it need?
everyday-stamp-try-opt-same: One stamp, the same as a letter
everyday-stamp-try-fb-same: A heavy box takes more work to deliver. Think about how the cost follows the work.
everyday-stamp-try-fb-more: Right. More work to deliver means more stamps.
everyday-stamp-try-opt-none: No stamp, since boxes ship free
everyday-stamp-try-fb-none: Nothing ships free. If it did, people could flood the post office with junk. Think about who pays for the work.
everyday-stamp-reveal-p1: In Ethereum, the stamp is a small fee paid in ETH, often called gas. Bigger jobs need more gas, and the fee stops anyone from flooding Ethereum with junk.
everyday-stamp-reveal-p2: Unlike a real stamp, the price of gas moves. It goes up when lots of people are using Ethereum at once, and back down when it's quieter.
everyday-stamp-amount-prompt: A check for a tiny amount and a check for a huge amount need the same envelope and the same stamp. So which pays the bigger fee: sending a little ETH, or a lot?
everyday-stamp-amount-fb-more: A bigger check doesn't need more stamps. Think about whether the work changes with the amount.
everyday-stamp-amount-fb-same: Right. The fee pays for the work of adding your payment, not for how much it moves. Sending a lot takes the same work as sending a little.
everyday-stamp-amount-fb-less: Small payments don't get cheaper stamps. Think about whether the work changes with the amount.
everyday-stamp-busy-prompt: Lots of people are using Ethereum right now, so fees are high. Your payment isn't urgent. What's a smart way to save?
everyday-stamp-busy-fb-skip: Every payment needs a fee, like every letter needs a stamp. Think about when fees cost less.
everyday-stamp-busy-opt-wait: Send it later, when Ethereum is quieter
everyday-stamp-busy-fb-wait: Right. Fees drop when fewer people are using Ethereum, so waiting can save you money.
everyday-stamp-busy-fb-small: Half a fee doesn't cover the job, so your payment won't go through. Think about when fees cost less.
everyday-stamp-takeaway-p1: Every payment on Ethereum pays a small fee in ETH, like a stamp. The fee follows the work, not the amount you send, and it rises when Ethereum is busy.
everyday-machine-summary: Programs on Ethereum that follow their rules exactly.
everyday-machine-picture-p1: A vending machine sells snacks without a shopkeeper. It follows the same rules for everyone: pay the right amount and the snack drops, or nothing happens.
everyday-machine-try-prompt: Buy a snack. Then try paying the wrong amount, or picking one that's sold out.
everyday-machine-try-explain: The machine followed its rules every time. Nobody behind a counter had to say yes or no.
everyday-machine-reveal-p1: In Ethereum, a program that works like this is called a smart contract: it follows its rules exactly, with no person in the middle. Apps on Ethereum are built from smart contracts.
everyday-machine-tickets-prompt: A smart contract sells concert tickets for ETH. You try to pay a little less than the price. What happens?
everyday-machine-tickets-opt-anyway: It sells you the ticket anyway, since you were close
everyday-machine-tickets-fb-anyway: Close isn't enough. The contract follows its rules exactly, the same way for everyone.
everyday-machine-tickets-opt-staff: Someone at the box office decides whether to let it slide
everyday-machine-tickets-fb-staff: There's no box office. The rules decide, with no person in the middle.
everyday-machine-tickets-opt-refused: It turns you down, and your ETH stays with you
everyday-machine-tickets-fb-refused: Right. Like the vending machine, it follows its rules for everyone. The payment never goes through, so your ETH stays at your address. Only the small fee is spent.
everyday-machine-takeaway-p1: A smart contract is like a vending machine on Ethereum: a program that follows its rules exactly, with no shopkeeper in the middle.
everyday-undo-summary: Why there are no take-backs, and how to keep your key safe.
everyday-undo-picture-p1: Once you hand someone cash, there's no undo button. And if you lose every copy of the key to an unbreakable safe, no help desk can make you a new one.
everyday-undo-try-prompt: Your safe has one key. You can copy it, but if every copy is lost, nobody can ever make another. How do you avoid getting locked out for good?
everyday-undo-try-opt-spare: Make a copy of the key and hide it where only you know
everyday-undo-try-fb-spare: Right. With a copy kept somewhere safe and secret, losing one key isn't the end.
everyday-undo-try-opt-stranger: Give a copy to a friendly stranger who offers to hold it
everyday-undo-try-fb-stranger: Whoever holds a copy can open your safe whenever they like. Think about who should know where it is.
everyday-undo-try-opt-maker: Call the safe maker if it happens
everyday-undo-try-fb-maker: Once every copy is gone, nobody can make another, not even the safe's maker. Make your copy before you need it.
everyday-undo-reveal-p1: In Ethereum, a payment is like cash: once sent, nobody can undo it. Your hidden copy of the key is a recovery phrase, a list of words that brings back your private key, so write it on paper and never share it.
everyday-undo-support-prompt: You'd never hand a stranger a copy of your safe's key. A message says: "Hi, I'm from wallet support. Send me your recovery phrase and I'll fix your account." What is it?
everyday-undo-support-opt-send: Real help, so you send the phrase
everyday-undo-support-fb-send: Real support never asks for your recovery phrase. Think about what anyone holding it could do.
everyday-undo-support-opt-half: Fine, as long as you send only half the words
everyday-undo-support-fb-half: Even part of the phrase helps a thief. Think about who really needs it.
everyday-undo-support-opt-scam: A scam: anyone with the phrase can take your ETH
everyday-undo-support-fb-scam: Right. Nobody genuine ever needs your recovery phrase. Anyone who asks for it is trying to take your ETH.
everyday-undo-takeaway-p1: Payments on Ethereum can't be undone, and no help desk can reset your key. Keep your recovery phrase safe, and never share it with anyone.
everyday-story-summary: One payment from start to finish, step by step.
everyday-story-picture-p1: Alex owes Sam for lunch and decides to pay Sam back in ETH. Follow the payment from start to finish.
everyday-story-try-item-address: Sam shares an address: the mailbox slot
everyday-story-try-item-fee: Alex enters it and sees the fee: the stamp
everyday-story-try-item-key: Alex approves with Alex's private key
everyday-story-try-item-notebook: A new line goes on the blockchain: the global notebook
everyday-story-try-item-arrives: Sam sees the ETH at Sam's address
everyday-story-try-explain: Every step had an everyday twin: a mailbox slot to send to, a stamp to pay for delivery, a key only Alex has, and a notebook the whole world shares.
everyday-story-reveal-p1: In Ethereum, that whole trip is called a transaction. A transaction is any change added to the notebook. Once it's on the blockchain, nobody can undo it, and anyone can see it.
everyday-story-twins-prompt: Match each Ethereum word to its everyday twin.
everyday-story-twins-match-blockchain: A notebook everyone keeps a copy of
everyday-story-twins-match-address: A mailbox slot anyone can use
everyday-story-twins-match-fee: A stamp that pays for delivery
everyday-story-twins-explain: Each everyday picture stands for one part of Ethereum, and every payment uses all of them.
everyday-story-takeaway-p1: A transaction brings it together: an address to send to, a fee, your private key to approve it, and the blockchain to record it for good.
everyday-exam-notebook-prompt: In Ethereum, what plays the part of the notebook that everyone keeps an identical copy of?
everyday-exam-notebook-explain: The blockchain is Ethereum's shared notebook. Computers all over the world keep identical copies of it, so an old line can't be quietly changed.
everyday-exam-change-prompt: Someone secretly edits an old line in their own copy of the blockchain. What happens?
everyday-exam-change-opt-counts: Their edit becomes the new record
everyday-exam-change-opt-spreads: Every other copy updates to match
everyday-exam-change-opt-ignored: The other copies still show the real line, so the edit is ignored
everyday-exam-change-explain: Every other copy still holds the real line, so an edit in one copy gets nowhere.
everyday-exam-cash-prompt: Sending ETH is most like which everyday way of paying?
everyday-exam-cash-opt-cash: Handing over cash, with no bank in between
everyday-exam-cash-opt-card: Paying by card, through your bank
everyday-exam-cash-opt-check: Writing a check that a bank has to clear
everyday-exam-cash-explain: Like cash, ETH goes straight from you to the other person, with no bank in the middle.
everyday-exam-slot-prompt: A mailbox slot lets anyone drop money in. What is its twin in Ethereum?
everyday-exam-slot-explain: Your address is like the slot: anyone can send ETH to it. Moving that ETH takes your private key.
everyday-exam-wallet-prompt: You have a wallet app on your phone. What does it keep for you?
everyday-exam-wallet-explain: Your wallet keeps your private key. Your ETH stays at your address on the blockchain.
everyday-exam-stamp-prompt: A stamp pays for delivering a letter, and heavier mail needs more of them. What is its twin in Ethereum?
everyday-exam-stamp-explain: Every payment on Ethereum carries a small fee in ETH. Bigger jobs cost more, and the price goes up when Ethereum is busy.
everyday-exam-machine-prompt: A vending machine follows its rules with no shopkeeper. What is its twin in Ethereum?
everyday-exam-machine-explain: A smart contract is a program on Ethereum that follows its rules exactly, with no person in the middle.
everyday-exam-undo-prompt: You sent ETH to the wrong address by mistake. Who can undo it?
everyday-exam-undo-opt-nobody: Nobody: once it's on the blockchain, it can't be undone
everyday-exam-undo-explain: A payment can't be undone once it's on the blockchain, so check the address before you send.
everyday-exam-spare-prompt: A hidden copy of your key gets you back into your safe. What is its twin in Ethereum?
everyday-exam-spare-explain: Your recovery phrase is a list of words that brings back your private key. Write it on paper and never share it.
everyday-exam-support-prompt: Someone online says they're from wallet support and asks for your recovery phrase to fix a problem. What is it?
everyday-exam-support-opt-send: Real help, so you share it
everyday-exam-support-opt-scam: A scam to take your ETH
everyday-exam-support-opt-half: Safe, as long as you share only half
everyday-exam-support-explain: Real support never asks for your recovery phrase. Anyone who has it can take your ETH.
wallets-description: Find out what a wallet really holds, why your recovery phrase matters, and how to keep both safe.
wallets-keys-title: Your wallet doesn't hold your ETH
wallets-keys-summary: Keys, addresses and where your money actually lives.
wallets-keys-intro-p1: Most people picture a wallet as a pouch that holds money. An Ethereum wallet works differently: your ETH, Ethereum's own money, never leaves the blockchain, a shared record of who owns what that thousands of computers keep in sync.
wallets-keys-intro-p2: What your wallet actually holds is a private key: a secret number that proves you're allowed to move the ETH recorded at your address, the public ID that others send ETH to.
wallets-keys-where-prompt: So where is your ETH right now?
wallets-keys-where-opt-app: Inside the wallet app on your phone
wallets-keys-where-fb-app: The app only stores your keys. Delete the app and your ETH is still on Ethereum, waiting for whoever holds the key.
wallets-keys-where-opt-chain: On the Ethereum blockchain, recorded under your address
wallets-keys-where-fb-chain: Exactly. Balances live on the blockchain, a shared record that thousands of computers keep in sync.
wallets-keys-where-opt-company: On the servers of the company that made the wallet
wallets-keys-where-fb-company: Not when you hold your own keys. The wallet maker never has your ETH, which also means it can't recover it for you.
wallets-keys-generate-prompt: Generate a private key and its address using the same math every Ethereum wallet uses. Then change a single character of the private key and watch what happens to the address.
wallets-keys-generate-explain: Your address is calculated from your private key, but the math only runs one way. Anyone can see your address, and nobody can work backwards to your key.
wallets-keys-share-prompt: A friend wants to send you some ETH. What should you give them?
wallets-keys-share-fb-key: Never share this. Anyone with your private key controls everything at your address.
wallets-keys-share-fb-address: Right. Your address is public by design, so anyone can send to it. Just know that anyone who has it can also see its balance and history.
wallets-keys-share-opt-both: Both, so the transfer goes through faster
wallets-keys-share-fb-both: A transfer only ever needs the recipient's address. Sharing your key would hand over control of your funds.
wallets-keys-takeaway-p1: Your address is like an email address: share it with anyone who needs to pay you, but know they can see its balance and history. Your private key is like the password: share it with no one.
wallets-recovery-summary: The words that can bring your wallet back, or give it away.
wallets-recovery-intro-p1: Private keys are long strings of characters that are easy to copy wrong. So most wallets show you a recovery phrase (also called a seed phrase) instead: usually 12 or 24 ordinary words.
wallets-recovery-intro-p2: Those words can recreate every key in your wallet, on any device, in any compatible wallet app.
wallets-recovery-lost-prompt: Your phone falls in a lake. You still have your recovery phrase written down. What happens to your ETH?
wallets-recovery-lost-fb-gone: Your ETH was never on the phone. Enter the phrase into a wallet on a new device and everything reappears.
wallets-recovery-lost-opt-restore: You restore your wallet on a new device using the phrase
wallets-recovery-lost-fb-restore: Yes. The phrase recreates your keys, and your keys unlock your ETH on the blockchain.
wallets-recovery-lost-opt-support: You contact the wallet's support team to restore it
wallets-recovery-lost-fb-support: When you hold your own keys, nobody else can restore your wallet for you. The phrase is the only way back in.
wallets-recovery-storage-prompt: Which of these are reasonable places to keep your recovery phrase?
wallets-recovery-storage-opt-paper: Written on paper, stored somewhere safe at home
wallets-recovery-storage-fb-paper: Offline and private. Just protect it from fire, water and curious visitors.
wallets-recovery-storage-opt-photo: A photo in your camera roll
wallets-recovery-storage-fb-photo: Photos often sync to cloud services automatically, so your phrase could end up on someone else's servers.
wallets-recovery-storage-opt-metal: Stamped into a metal backup plate
wallets-recovery-storage-fb-metal: A metal backup survives fire and flood, and it never touches the internet.
wallets-recovery-storage-opt-email: A note in your email drafts
wallets-recovery-storage-fb-email: If your email account is ever compromised, your wallet goes with it.
wallets-recovery-storage-explain: Both good options keep the phrase offline. Anything stored on an internet-connected account can be stolen remotely.
wallets-recovery-scam-prompt: Someone claiming to be wallet support messages you and asks for your recovery phrase to "verify your account". What do you do?
wallets-recovery-scam-opt-send: Send it, since they're from support
wallets-recovery-scam-fb-send: This is one of the most common wallet scams. Real support will never ask for your phrase.
wallets-recovery-scam-opt-half: Send only the first half, to be safe
wallets-recovery-scam-fb-half: Even part of a phrase makes the rest far easier to guess. Never share any of it.
wallets-recovery-scam-opt-refuse: Refuse. Nobody legitimate ever needs it
wallets-recovery-scam-fb-refuse: Exactly. Anyone asking for your recovery phrase is trying to take your funds.
wallets-recovery-takeaway-p1: Whoever has your recovery phrase owns your wallet. Write it down offline, keep it private, and never type it into a website or send it to anyone.
transactions-description: See what really happens when you press send, and learn how gas fees work before you pay one.
transactions-lifecycle-title: What happens when you hit send
transactions-lifecycle-summary: From a signature in your wallet to a permanent record on the blockchain.
transactions-lifecycle-intro-p1: Sending ETH isn't like sending an email. Your wallet builds a message that says who's sending, who's receiving and how much, then signs it with your private key.
transactions-lifecycle-intro-p2: That signature proves the transaction came from you, without revealing your key. Your wallet then broadcasts it: sends it out to the computers that run the network.
transactions-lifecycle-order-prompt: Put the life of a transaction in order.
transactions-lifecycle-order-item-create: You enter an address and an amount
transactions-lifecycle-order-item-sign: Your wallet signs the transaction with your private key
transactions-lifecycle-order-item-broadc: The signed transaction is broadcast to the network
transactions-lifecycle-order-item-includ: A validator, one of the computers that run the network, adds it to a new block
transactions-lifecycle-order-item-confir: The block joins the chain and balances update
transactions-lifecycle-order-explain: Each step depends on the one before it: no signature, no broadcast. No block, no balance change.
transactions-lifecycle-undo-prompt: Your transaction has been included in a block. Can you undo it?
transactions-lifecycle-undo-fb-support: There's no Ethereum support desk with an undo button. No central party controls the network.
transactions-lifecycle-undo-fb-window: There's no undo window, and no clock that runs out. Time doesn't change what's on chain.
transactions-lifecycle-undo-opt-final: No. Once it's on chain, it can't be reversed
transactions-lifecycle-undo-fb-final: Right. That's why it pays to double-check the address before you sign.
transactions-lifecycle-takeaway-p1: A transaction is a signed instruction. Once it's in a block, you can't take it back, so always check the address and amount before you sign.
transactions-gas-summary: Why every transaction has a fee, and how to keep it low.
transactions-gas-intro-p1: Every transaction uses computing power from the network. Gas measures that work, and you pay a fee for it in ETH.
transactions-gas-intro-p2: The fee is the gas used times the gas price, quoted in gwei, a billionth of an ETH. The price is a base fee set by the network plus an optional tip for validators. Your wallet also sets a gas limit: the most gas the transaction is allowed to use.
transactions-gas-calculator-prompt: A simple ETH transfer uses 21,000 gas. Set the gas price so the fee matches the goal.
transactions-gas-calculator-explain: Fee = gas used × gas price. Prices are quoted in gwei, one billionth of an ETH, and are made up of a base fee set by the network plus an optional tip for validators.
transactions-gas-compare-prompt: Using an app to trade one currency for another often takes more than 100,000 gas, while a simple transfer uses 21,000. At the same gas price, which costs more?
transactions-gas-compare-fb-transfer: The transfer uses the least gas of any transaction, so at the same price it's the cheapest.
transactions-gas-compare-fb-swap: Right. More complex transactions do more computing work, so they use more gas and cost more.
transactions-gas-compare-fb-same: Fees scale with the gas used, so more work means a bigger fee.
transactions-gas-cheaper-prompt: Your transaction isn't urgent. What's the best way to pay less?
transactions-gas-cheaper-opt-limit: Set a gas limit below what the transaction needs
transactions-gas-cheaper-fb-limit: If the limit is too low, the transaction runs out of gas and fails, and you still pay for the work done.
transactions-gas-cheaper-opt-currency: Pay the fee in a different currency
transactions-gas-cheaper-fb-currency: On Ethereum, gas fees are always paid in ETH.
transactions-gas-cheaper-opt-wait: Wait for a quieter time, when demand is lower
transactions-gas-cheaper-fb-wait: Exactly. Lower demand means a lower base fee.
transactions-gas-takeaway-p1: Fee = gas used × gas price. Simple transactions use less gas, and quieter times mean lower prices.

wallets-signing-summary: How your key approves things without ever leaving your wallet.
wallets-signing-intro-p1: Every time you approve something in your wallet, it creates a digital signature: a code that only your private key could have produced.
wallets-signing-intro-p2: Anyone can check a signature against your address, but nobody can use it to work out your key or sign something new.
wallets-signing-proves-prompt: When you sign a message, what does the signature prove?
wallets-signing-proves-fb-identity: A signature proves control of a key, not who you are in the real world.
wallets-signing-proves-opt-key: That whoever holds the key for your address approved this exact message
wallets-signing-proves-fb-key: Right. And it covers this exact message only. Let's see what happens if someone changes it.
wallets-signing-proves-opt-secret: That the message is encrypted and hidden
wallets-signing-proves-fb-secret: Signing doesn't hide anything. The message stays readable; the signature proves who approved it.
wallets-signing-sign-prompt: Sign a message with a demo key and send it out. Then play the attacker: change the message, or try to fake the signature, and see whether it still checks out.
wallets-signing-sign-explain: Your key signs offline, and only the message and signature go out. Anyone can check them without your key, but change a single character, or sign with any other key, and it no longer matches your address.
wallets-signing-blind-prompt: A site you've never heard of asks you to sign a message full of unreadable code to "claim a free prize". What do you do?
wallets-signing-blind-opt-sign: Sign it. Signing doesn't send anything, so it's harmless
wallets-signing-blind-fb-sign: Some signatures give a site permission to move your assets. Signing something you can't read can hand them over.
wallets-signing-blind-opt-reject: Reject it. Never sign anything you can't read or didn't expect
wallets-signing-blind-fb-reject: Exactly. If you can't tell what you're approving, the safe answer is no.
wallets-signing-blind-opt-padlock: Sign it, since the site looks professional and has a padlock in the address bar
wallets-signing-blind-fb-padlock: Scam sites can look polished and use a padlock too. The padlock only means the connection is private, not that the site is honest.
wallets-signing-takeaway-p1: A signature is your key saying yes to one exact message. Only sign things you can read, understand and expect.
wallets-addresses-summary: One phrase, many accounts, and how to be sure you're sending to the right one.
wallets-addresses-intro-p1: Your recovery phrase can create more than one key. Most wallets let you add extra accounts from the same phrase, each with its own private key and its own address.
wallets-addresses-intro-p2: Any of those addresses is safe to share, in that nobody can spend from it. It isn't private, though: anyone who has it can look up its balance and every transfer, one reason people keep separate accounts for different uses. Sending is where care matters most: once ETH goes to the wrong address, nobody can undo the transfer for you.
wallets-addresses-ends-prompt: Addresses are long, so many wallets show only the first and last few characters. Is matching those enough to know you have the right address?
wallets-addresses-ends-opt-enough: Yes. Two different addresses almost never share both ends
wallets-addresses-ends-fb-enough: By chance, rarely. But someone can create addresses on purpose until one starts and ends just like a real one.
wallets-addresses-ends-opt-warn: Yes. Your wallet would warn you about a wrong address
wallets-addresses-ends-fb-warn: Your wallet can't know who you meant to pay. Some wallets flag new or look-alike addresses, but a look-alike is a real, working address, so the transfer can still go through.
wallets-addresses-ends-opt-middle: No. The characters in the middle could be different
wallets-addresses-ends-fb-middle: Right. The middle is where a look-alike hides. Try spotting one in the next step.
wallets-addresses-spot-prompt: Sam sends you their address so you can pay them back. Which address below matches it exactly?
wallets-addresses-spot-explain: All four addresses start and end the same way, so the shortened view can't tell them apart. Only checking the whole address catches a look-alike.
wallets-addresses-poison-prompt: A tiny amount arrives in your wallet from an address that starts and ends just like your friend Ana's. Later, you want to pay Ana. What should you do?
wallets-addresses-poison-opt-history: Copy Ana's address from your recent activity, since that's quickest
wallets-addresses-poison-fb-history: That's what the sender is counting on. The look-alike now sits in your activity, easy to copy by mistake.
wallets-addresses-poison-opt-ends: Check that the first and last few characters match, then send
wallets-addresses-poison-fb-ends: Those are exactly the characters the look-alike copied. A glance at the ends will happily approve the fake.
wallets-addresses-poison-opt-source: Use the address Ana gave you, or a contact you saved earlier, and check it in full
wallets-addresses-poison-fb-source: Right. This trick is called address poisoning: a look-alike planted in your activity in the hope you'll copy it. Going back to a source you trust avoids it.
wallets-addresses-wrong-prompt: You send ETH, then notice the address was wrong. What can you do?
wallets-addresses-wrong-opt-support: Ask Ethereum's support team to reverse it
wallets-addresses-wrong-fb-support: Ethereum has no central authority that can reverse a transfer. Anyone who says they can is probably running a scam.
wallets-addresses-wrong-opt-bounce: Wait. It bounces back if nobody uses that address
wallets-addresses-wrong-fb-bounce: Transfers don't bounce. ETH sent to a valid address stays there, whether anyone uses it or not.
wallets-addresses-wrong-opt-owner: Ask whoever owns that address to send it back, if you know who they are
wallets-addresses-wrong-fb-owner: That's the only way. Only the holder of that address's private key can move the ETH, which is why checking before you send matters so much. Never type an address by hand: copy it from a source you trust.
wallets-addresses-verify-text: A look-alike address copies the {b1} of a real one, so check the {b2} address against one you trust before you send.
wallets-addresses-verify-explain: Look-alikes are made to match the few characters a wallet shows at each end. Only checking every character against an address you trust catches the difference in the middle.
wallets-addresses-takeaway-p1: Sharing your address lets people see its activity, but never spend from it. Sending is final: check the whole address against one you trust, not just the start and end.
wallets-custody-summary: Exchanges, phone apps and hardware wallets: who's really in control.
wallets-custody-intro-p1: So far, this course has assumed you hold your own keys. Many people start on an exchange instead: a company that lets you buy and sell ETH. There, the company holds the keys for you. That's a custodial account: an account with the company, where someone else holds your keys.
wallets-custody-intro-p2: It's convenient. You sign in with a password, and support can help if you forget it. But the company controls the funds: it can freeze your account, and exchanges have failed and lost their customers' money.
wallets-custody-control-prompt: Your exchange suddenly stops letting customers take their ETH out. Who can move the ETH in your account there?
wallets-custody-control-opt-password: You can, with your exchange password
wallets-custody-control-fb-password: Your password only signs you in to the company's website. It isn't a private key, so it can't move anything on its own.
wallets-custody-control-opt-exchange: Only the exchange, because it holds the keys
wallets-custody-control-fb-exchange: Right. Whoever holds the keys controls the funds, and here that's the company.
wallets-custody-control-opt-phrase: You can, using your recovery phrase
wallets-custody-control-fb-phrase: A custodial account doesn't give you a recovery phrase for those funds. The keys stay with the company.
wallets-custody-storage-p1: Holding your own keys comes with choices too. A wallet app on your phone or computer is a hot wallet: its keys live on a device that's connected to the internet. That's handy for everyday use, but a hacked device could expose them.
wallets-custody-storage-p2: A hardware wallet is a small device made to keep keys offline, which makes it a cold wallet. It signs on the device itself, so your private key never touches the internet, even while it's plugged into a computer.
wallets-custody-sort-prompt: Sort each situation by who holds the keys, and whether they're kept online or offline.
wallets-custody-sort-explain: Custodial means someone else holds the keys. When you hold them yourself, a hot wallet keeps them on an internet-connected device, and a hardware wallet keeps them offline, even while it's plugged in.
wallets-custody-savings-prompt: You're saving ETH for years and will rarely touch it. Which setup fits best?
wallets-custody-savings-opt-exchange: Leave it on the exchange where you bought it
wallets-custody-savings-fb-exchange: Easy, but the exchange stays in control the whole time. If it freezes your account or fails, your savings go with it.
wallets-custody-savings-opt-hardware: A hardware wallet, with its recovery phrase written down and stored offline
wallets-custody-savings-fb-hardware: Right. Offline keys are much harder to steal, and the recovery phrase brings everything back if the device breaks or gets lost.
wallets-custody-savings-opt-phone: A wallet app on your phone, since it's always with you
wallets-custody-savings-fb-phone: Great for everyday spending, but those keys live on an internet-connected device. For savings you rarely touch, offline keys are safer.
wallets-custody-match-prompt: Match each term to what it means.
wallets-custody-match-match-hot: Your keys on an internet-connected device
wallets-custody-match-match-hardware: Small device keeping your keys offline
wallets-custody-match-match-phrase: Words that can recreate your keys
wallets-custody-match-explain: Whoever holds the keys controls the ETH. A custodial account leaves them with someone else. If you hold your own, a hot wallet keeps them online, a hardware wallet keeps them offline, and your recovery phrase can bring them back.
wallets-custody-takeaway-p1: Whoever holds the keys controls the ETH. Hold your own, and keep the keys to long-term savings offline.
wallets-exam-balance-prompt: You delete your wallet app by mistake. Where is your ETH while the app is gone?
wallets-exam-balance-opt-chain: On the Ethereum blockchain, still recorded under your address
wallets-exam-balance-opt-maker: On the wallet maker's servers, until you reinstall
wallets-exam-balance-explain: A wallet holds keys, not coins. Your ETH stays on the blockchain under your address, ready for whoever holds the key.
wallets-exam-public-prompt: You post your address on a public page so people can pay you. What can a stranger do with it?
wallets-exam-public-opt-move: Move the ETH recorded at it
wallets-exam-public-opt-key: Work out your private key from it
wallets-exam-public-explain: An address is public by design, so anyone can send to it. Moving ETH takes the private key, and the math that turns a key into an address only runs one way. Anyone who has your address can also see its balance and history.
wallets-exam-restore-prompt: Your laptop stops working for good, and your wallet app was on it. Your recovery phrase is written down at home. How do you get back to your ETH?
wallets-exam-restore-opt-support: Ask the wallet app's support team to restore your account
wallets-exam-restore-opt-gone: You can't. The ETH was stored on the laptop
wallets-exam-restore-opt-phrase: Enter the phrase into a wallet app on another device
wallets-exam-restore-explain: Your ETH never left the blockchain. The recovery phrase recreates your keys in any compatible wallet app, on any device.
wallets-exam-website-prompt: A pop-up on a website warns that your wallet is at risk and asks you to type in your recovery phrase to secure it. What should you do?
wallets-exam-website-opt-type: Type it in. The pop-up is there to protect your wallet
wallets-exam-website-opt-close: Close the page. Nobody legitimate ever needs your phrase
wallets-exam-website-opt-part: Type in only the first few words, to be safe
wallets-exam-website-explain: Whoever has your recovery phrase owns your wallet, so any request for it is an attempt to take your funds. Even part of the phrase makes the rest far easier to guess.
wallets-exam-signature-prompt: Which of these are true of a digital signature?
wallets-exam-signature-opt-identity: It proves your real name and identity
wallets-exam-signature-opt-key: Only your private key could have produced it
wallets-exam-signature-opt-reveal: Anyone who sees it can use it to work out your private key
wallets-exam-signature-opt-exact: It covers one exact message, and stops matching if the message changes
wallets-exam-signature-explain: A signature is made by your private key and tied to one exact message. It proves control of a key, not who you are, and nobody can use it to work out the key.
wallets-exam-unreadable-prompt: A site you don't know asks you to sign a request you can't make sense of, to unlock a "free bonus". It says signing is harmless because nothing is being sent. What do you do?
wallets-exam-unreadable-opt-reject: Reject it. Don't sign anything you can't read or didn't expect
wallets-exam-unreadable-opt-sign: Sign it. A signature can't give anyone access to your assets
wallets-exam-unreadable-opt-padlock: Sign it, since the site looks professional and has a padlock in the address bar
wallets-exam-unreadable-explain: Some signatures give a site permission to move your assets, so signing something you can't read could hand them over. If you can't tell what you're approving, the safe answer is no.
wallets-exam-lookalike-prompt: You want to pay your landlord, Jo, in ETH. Your recent activity shows an address that starts and ends just like Jo's. Where should the address you pay come from?
wallets-exam-lookalike-opt-recent: Your recent activity, since it's already in your wallet
wallets-exam-lookalike-opt-trusted: The address Jo gave you, or a contact you saved earlier, checked in full
wallets-exam-lookalike-opt-ends: Any copy you find, as long as its first and last few characters match Jo's
wallets-exam-lookalike-explain: Look-alike addresses copy the start and end of a real one, and address poisoning plants them in your activity. Going back to a source you trust and checking the whole address avoids paying a stranger.
wallets-exam-mistake-prompt: You sent ETH to an address with one wrong character. Who can move that ETH now?
wallets-exam-mistake-opt-holder: Only whoever holds the private key for that address
wallets-exam-mistake-opt-support: Ethereum's support team, if you ask quickly
wallets-exam-mistake-opt-bounce: Nobody needs to. It returns to you if the address is never used
wallets-exam-mistake-explain: Transfers are final: they don't bounce, and no central authority can reverse them. Only the holder of that address's private key can move the ETH, and for a mistyped address that is almost certainly nobody, so it's lost for good. Never type an address by hand: copy it from a source you trust.
wallets-exam-frozen-prompt: You keep ETH on an exchange, and it freezes every customer's account. What can you do with your ETH there?
wallets-exam-frozen-opt-password: Move it out by signing in with your password
wallets-exam-frozen-opt-phrase: Move it out with your recovery phrase
wallets-exam-frozen-opt-exchange: Nothing on your own. The exchange holds the keys
wallets-exam-frozen-explain: An exchange account is custodial: the company holds the keys, so it controls the funds. Your password only signs you in to its website, and you have no recovery phrase for that ETH.
wallets-exam-savings-prompt: You keep a little ETH for everyday payments and a larger amount you won't touch for years. Which setup fits best?
wallets-exam-savings-opt-phone: Everything in a wallet app on your phone, so it's all in one place
wallets-exam-savings-opt-split: A phone wallet app for everyday spending, and a hardware wallet for the savings
wallets-exam-savings-opt-exchange: Everything on an exchange, so support can help if you forget your password
wallets-exam-savings-explain: A hot wallet on your phone is handy for spending, but its keys sit on an internet-connected device. Savings you rarely touch are safer on a hardware wallet, which keeps your own keys offline.
transactions-blocks-summary: Play validator and decide which transactions make the cut.
transactions-blocks-intro-p1: Transactions don't land on the blockchain one at a time. Validators, who stake ETH to run the network, bundle them into blocks, with a chance for a new block every 12 seconds.
transactions-blocks-intro-p2: Each block has limited space, measured in gas. When more transactions are waiting than will fit, the validator chooses which ones go in.
transactions-blocks-build-prompt: You're the validator. Fill the block from the waiting pool to hit the tip goal without overfilling the block.
transactions-blocks-build-explain: Validators keep the tip on every transaction they include, so the ones paying the most per unit of gas get picked first. The base fee is burned (destroyed for good), so it doesn't affect the choice.
transactions-blocks-priority-prompt: The network is busy and you need your transaction in the next block. What helps most?
transactions-blocks-priority-fb-limit: The limit only caps how much gas you'll allow. Set it too low and the transaction fails, and you still pay.
transactions-blocks-priority-fb-tip: Right. A higher tip moves you up the validator's list.
transactions-blocks-priority-opt-resend: Press send again a few times
transactions-blocks-priority-fb-resend: Each time you press send, your wallet makes a new transaction. Several could go through, and you'd pay several times, each with its own fee.
transactions-blocks-final-prompt: Your transaction is in a block. When is it truly permanent?
transactions-blocks-final-fb-instant: Inclusion is a very good sign, but a brand-new block can, rarely, still be replaced.
transactions-blocks-final-opt-never: Never. Blockchains can always be rewritten
transactions-blocks-final-fb-never: Even blockchains have a point of no return. Reversing a block past it would cost an attacker at least a third of all staked ETH.
transactions-blocks-final-opt-finalized: Once the network finalizes it, about 13 to 19 minutes later
transactions-blocks-final-fb-finalized: Exactly. Once a block is finalized, undoing it would destroy a huge amount of staked ETH.
transactions-blocks-match-up-prompt: Match each term to the right description.
transactions-blocks-match-up-match-tip: Kept by the validator who includes it
transactions-blocks-match-up-match-base: Burned, so no one receives it
transactions-blocks-match-up-match-space: Limited, so validators choose what fits
transactions-blocks-match-up-match-final: Undoing it would get validators slashed
transactions-blocks-match-up-explain: Validators keep the tips and the base fee is burned, so tips decide who gets the limited space. Once a block is finalized, undoing it would cost validators a huge amount of staked ETH.
transactions-blocks-takeaway-p1: Blocks have limited space, validators pick the best-paying transactions first, and a finalized block is permanent.
transactions-failed-summary: Why a failed transaction still costs a fee, and how the gas limit protects you.
transactions-failed-intro-p1: Making it into a block doesn't always mean a transaction worked. A failed transaction is included in a block but doesn't finish: for example, it runs out of gas partway through, or the app it's using rejects it.
transactions-failed-intro-p2: When that happens, everything the transaction tried to change is undone, as if it had never run. The trade doesn't happen, and the amount you tried to send stays put.
transactions-failed-predict-prompt: Your transaction failed, and everything it tried to do was undone. Does it still cost you anything?
transactions-failed-predict-opt-free: No. It was undone, so there's nothing to pay
transactions-failed-predict-fb-free: Undoing the changes doesn't undo the work. Validators still ran the transaction up to the point it failed, and that work has a cost.
transactions-failed-predict-opt-fee: Yes. You still pay for the gas it used
transactions-failed-predict-fb-fee: Right. Validators did the work of running it, so the fee is still paid, even though the result was undone. Test it in the next step.
transactions-failed-predict-opt-later: Yes, but the fee comes back once the network sees it failed
transactions-failed-predict-fb-later: Failing doesn't earn a refund. The gas the transaction used was real work, so that part of the fee stays spent.
transactions-failed-limit-prompt: This trade's exact gas need is hidden. Find the lowest gas limit at which it goes through.
transactions-failed-limit-explain: The trade needs 130,000 gas. Any lower limit runs out partway, and you pay for all the gas it used anyway. Any limit at or above it costs the same, because gas left unused under the limit is refunded.
transactions-failed-headroom-prompt: Your wallet suggests a gas limit of 200,000 for a trade that usually uses about 120,000. What should you do?
transactions-failed-headroom-opt-lower: Lower it to 100,000 to cut the fee
transactions-failed-headroom-fb-lower: The fee depends on the gas used, not the limit, so this saves nothing. Below what the trade needs, it fails and you still pay.
transactions-failed-headroom-opt-exact: Set it to exactly 120,000 so you don't overpay
transactions-failed-headroom-fb-exact: There's nothing to overpay: unused gas is refunded. And if the trade needs a little more than usual this time, it fails and you still pay.
transactions-failed-headroom-fb-keep: Right. The extra room adds nothing to the fee, because you only pay for the gas actually used, and it keeps the trade from running out.
transactions-failed-undone-prompt: You tried to send 0.5 ETH to a trading app, and the transaction failed. What happened to the 0.5 ETH?
transactions-failed-undone-opt-lost: It's gone, along with the fee
transactions-failed-undone-fb-lost: Failure undoes every change the transaction tried to make, and moving your ETH was one of them.
transactions-failed-undone-opt-kept: It stayed with you. Only the fee was spent
transactions-failed-undone-fb-kept: Right. The failed transaction was undone, so the 0.5 ETH never left. The fee paid for the work done before it failed.
transactions-failed-undone-opt-retry: It's on hold until the network tries again
transactions-failed-undone-fb-retry: Nothing retries a failed transaction: its result is already recorded in a block. To try again, you send a new transaction.
transactions-failed-recap-prompt: Fill in what happens when a transaction fails.
transactions-failed-recap-text: When a transaction fails, its changes are {b1}, but you still pay for the gas it {b2}. Any gas left over under the limit is {b3}.
transactions-failed-recap-explain: Failing undoes the changes but not the work, so the gas used is still paid. Leftover gas under the limit comes back, which is why headroom in the limit is free.
transactions-failed-takeaway-p1: A failed transaction is undone but still costs the gas it used. Leave room in the gas limit: unused gas is refunded, so the headroom is free.
transactions-explorer-summary: Look up any transaction yourself and see whether it really worked.
transactions-explorer-intro-p1: Everything on Ethereum is public. A block explorer is a website that shows what's on the chain: every block, every address and every transaction, for anyone to look up.
transactions-explorer-intro-p2: Each transaction has a transaction hash: its unique ID, made by hashing the transaction's data into a short fingerprint. Your wallet can show it once you send, and searching for it on an explorer brings up the record.
transactions-explorer-proof-prompt: A seller won't ship until your payment arrives, and you sent it a minute ago. What's the most trustworthy thing to give them?
transactions-explorer-proof-opt-screensh: A screenshot of your wallet saying it was sent
transactions-explorer-proof-fb-screensho: Screenshots are easy to fake, and "sent" only means broadcast. It doesn't show the transaction made it into a block, or that it worked.
transactions-explorer-proof-fb-hash: Right. Anyone can look the hash up on a block explorer and check the result themselves, instead of trusting your screenshot.
transactions-explorer-proof-opt-balance: A screenshot of your lower balance
transactions-explorer-proof-fb-balance: A lower balance doesn't say where the ETH went, and even a failed transaction lowers it, because the fee is still paid.
transactions-explorer-read-prompt: Your wallet says your trade of 0.5 ETH was sent, but nothing came back from the trading app. Which field on this page proves the trade failed?
transactions-explorer-read-explain: Status is the field to trust. Being in a block, showing a value and charging a fee all happen to failed transactions too.
transactions-explorer-pending-prompt: You look up your transaction hash and the status says Pending. What does that mean?
transactions-explorer-pending-fb-failed: Failure has its own status, and a failed transaction is already in a block. Pending comes earlier than that.
transactions-explorer-pending-opt-waitin: It's been broadcast but isn't in a block yet
transactions-explorer-pending-fb-waiting: Right. It's waiting for a validator to include it. When the network is busy that can take a while, and a higher tip helps.
transactions-explorer-pending-opt-lost: The network lost it, so you should send it again
transactions-explorer-pending-fb-lost: Pending isn't lost. Sending again makes a second transaction, and if both go through, you pay twice.
transactions-explorer-public-prompt: Who can look up your transactions on a block explorer?
transactions-explorer-public-opt-you: Only you, using your private key
transactions-explorer-public-fb-you: Your private key is for signing, not reading. Looking up a transaction needs no key at all.
transactions-explorer-public-opt-both: Only you and the people you've paid
transactions-explorer-public-fb-both: There's no list of who's allowed to look. Ethereum's records aren't shared only with the people involved.
transactions-explorer-public-fb-anyone: Right. The chain is public, so anyone who knows your address can see its whole history. That's worth remembering before you share it.
transactions-explorer-takeaway-p1: To find out whether a transaction worked, look up its hash on a block explorer and read the status. Don't settle for a screenshot.
transactions-exam-sign-prompt: What has to happen before your transaction can be broadcast to the network?
transactions-exam-sign-opt-block: A validator puts it in a block
transactions-exam-sign-opt-key: Your wallet attaches your private key so the network knows it's you
transactions-exam-sign-opt-sign: Your wallet signs it with your private key
transactions-exam-sign-explain: Your wallet signs the transaction first, which proves it came from you without revealing your key. Only then is it broadcast, and later a validator includes it in a block.
transactions-exam-undo-prompt: A friend says there's no need to double-check an address, because a payment to the wrong one can be undone. What's true?
transactions-exam-undo-opt-final: Once a payment is on chain, nobody can reverse it
transactions-exam-undo-opt-support: Ethereum support can reverse it on request
transactions-exam-undo-opt-window: It can be cancelled within 24 hours
transactions-exam-undo-explain: No central party controls Ethereum and there's no undo window, so a transaction on chain stays there. That's why you check the address and amount before you sign.
transactions-exam-fee-prompt: A trade on an app uses 100,000 gas, and the gas price is 2 gwei. What's the fee?
transactions-exam-fee-explain: Fee = gas used × gas price, so 100,000 × 2 = 200,000 gwei. The trade does more work than a simple transfer, which uses 21,000 gas, so it costs more at the same price.
transactions-exam-wait-prompt: You want to send ETH to a friend sometime this week, but the network is busy right now. How can you pay a smaller fee?
transactions-exam-wait-opt-currency: Pay the fee in another currency instead of ETH
transactions-exam-wait-opt-limit: Set the gas limit lower than the transfer needs
transactions-exam-wait-opt-wait: Send it later, when fewer people are transacting
transactions-exam-wait-explain: Gas prices rise with demand, so a quieter time means a lower base fee. Fees on Ethereum are always paid in ETH, and a gas limit that's too low just makes the transaction fail.
transactions-exam-tip-prompt: The network is busy and your transaction is still waiting. Why does raising your tip help?
transactions-exam-tip-opt-keep: Validators keep the tip, so they pick the best-paying transactions first
transactions-exam-tip-opt-burn: The tip is burned, and the network moves transactions that burn more to the front
transactions-exam-tip-opt-limit: A higher tip raises your gas limit, giving the transaction more room
transactions-exam-tip-explain: Validators keep the tip on every transaction they include, so when there are more waiting than will fit, they pick the ones paying the most per unit of gas. The base fee is burned, so it doesn't sway their choice.
transactions-exam-final-prompt: Your payment was included in a block a few seconds ago. How permanent is it?
transactions-exam-final-opt-instant: Fully permanent from the moment it was included
transactions-exam-final-opt-finalized: Likely to stay now, and permanent once finalized, about 13 to 19 minutes later
transactions-exam-final-opt-never: Never fully permanent, because blockchains can always be rewritten
transactions-exam-final-explain: A brand-new block can, rarely, still be replaced. Once it's finalized, about 13 to 19 minutes later, undoing it would mean validators holding at least a third of all staked ETH breaking the rules and being slashed.
transactions-exam-outcome-prompt: Your trade on an app was included in a block, but it failed. What happened?
transactions-exam-outcome-opt-sent: The ETH you were trading still went to the app
transactions-exam-outcome-opt-fee: You paid for the gas it used
transactions-exam-outcome-opt-refund: The fee was refunded, because the trade failed
transactions-exam-outcome-opt-undone: Everything the trade tried to change was undone
transactions-exam-outcome-explain: A failed transaction is undone as if it never ran, so your ETH stays put. Validators still did the work of running it, so you pay for the gas it used.
transactions-exam-headroom-prompt: A trade needs exactly 130,000 gas. At the same gas price, how does its fee with a 200,000 gas limit compare to its fee with a 130,000 limit?
transactions-exam-headroom-opt-higher: Higher, because you pay for the whole limit
transactions-exam-headroom-opt-same: The same, because unused gas is refunded
transactions-exam-headroom-opt-fails: The 200,000 limit makes the trade fail, because the limit has to match its need exactly
transactions-exam-headroom-explain: You only pay for the gas the trade actually uses, and gas left unused under the limit is refunded. That makes extra room in the limit free, and it keeps the trade from running out.
transactions-exam-proof-prompt: You paid a friend back, and they want to check for themselves that the payment worked. What should you send them?
transactions-exam-proof-opt-screenshot: A screenshot of your wallet showing it was sent
transactions-exam-proof-opt-key: Your private key, so they can look inside your wallet
transactions-exam-proof-explain: Anyone can look up a transaction hash on a block explorer and read the result straight from the chain. Screenshots are easy to fake, and looking up a transaction needs no key at all.
transactions-exam-status-prompt: You look up a trade on a block explorer. Which field tells you whether it actually worked?
transactions-exam-status-explain: Status is the field to trust. Failed transactions are in a block too, still show the value they tried to send and still charge a fee.
blockchain-description: Play with hashes, break a chain, then try to attack the network. Learn why tampering doesn't pay.
blockchain-hashing-summary: Hash functions and why a tiny change changes everything.
blockchain-hashing-intro-p1: A hash function turns any data, a single word or a whole book, into a short, fixed-length code called a hash. Think of it as a fingerprint for data.
blockchain-hashing-intro-p2: Ethereum uses a hash function called Keccak-256. The same input always gives the same hash, on every computer in the world.
blockchain-hashing-predict-prompt: Make a prediction: if you change a single letter of the input, how much of the hash changes?
blockchain-hashing-predict-fb-one: It feels like it should. Test it in the next step.
blockchain-hashing-predict-fb-few: Good guess. Test it in the next step.
blockchain-hashing-predict-fb-most: Good instinct. Test it in the next step.
blockchain-hashing-playground-prompt: Type anything and watch its fingerprint. Then change just one character.
blockchain-hashing-playground-explain: A tiny change produces a completely different hash. That makes hashes perfect for spotting tampering: if the data changes, the fingerprint no longer matches.
blockchain-hashing-reverse-prompt: Someone hands you a hash. Can you work out the original input from it?
blockchain-hashing-reverse-opt-backwards: Yes, by running the function backwards
blockchain-hashing-reverse-fb-backwards: Hash functions only run one way. There's no backwards button.
blockchain-hashing-reverse-fb-supercompu: Even the fastest computers can't reverse a good hash. That one-way property is what makes it useful.
blockchain-hashing-reverse-opt-no: No, not in any practical amount of time
blockchain-hashing-reverse-fb-no: Right. The only approach is guessing inputs one by one, which is hopeless for anything but very short inputs.
blockchain-hashing-takeaway-p1: A hash is a one-way fingerprint: easy to compute, practically impossible to reverse, and completely different if the data changes even slightly.
blockchain-chain-summary: Why editing an old block gives the game away.
blockchain-chain-intro-p1: A blockchain groups its records into batches called blocks. Each block stores the hash of the block before it, linking them into a chain all the way back to the very first one.
blockchain-chain-intro-p2: Change anything in an old block and its hash changes, so the next block's link no longer matches.
blockchain-chain-tamper-prompt: Here's a tiny blockchain. Edit the data in block 1 and watch the links. Then try to repair the chain.
blockchain-chain-tamper-explain: Fixing one block breaks the next one, so rewriting history means redoing every later block and then convincing the rest of the network to accept your version.
blockchain-chain-detect-prompt: Thousands of computers, called nodes, each keep a copy of the chain. One copy has an edited old block. What happens?
blockchain-chain-detect-opt-accepted: Everyone switches to the edited copy
blockchain-chain-detect-fb-accepted: Nodes don't switch to a copy just because it exists. Each one checks the links for itself.
blockchain-chain-detect-fb-unnoticed: Checking hashes takes a computer milliseconds, and nodes check every block they receive.
blockchain-chain-detect-opt-rejected: Other nodes spot the broken links and reject it
blockchain-chain-detect-fb-rejected: Exactly. Anyone can check the links, so tampering is obvious.
blockchain-chain-takeaway-p1: Each block locks in the one before it. Editing history breaks the next link, and fixing it means rewriting every later block, so everyone can see it.
blockchain-consensus-summary: Staking, voting and what it would take to cheat.
blockchain-consensus-intro-p1: With thousands of computers keeping copies, who decides which block comes next? On Ethereum, validators do. Each one locks up, or stakes, ETH, Ethereum's own money, as a security deposit.
blockchain-consensus-intro-p2: For each block, one validator is picked at random to propose it, and others vote on it. Once validators holding two-thirds of all staked ETH agree, a block becomes final: locked in, because changing it would cost an attacker a huge amount of staked ETH.
blockchain-consensus-attack-prompt: An attacker wants to stop the chain from finalizing. Use the slider to find the smallest share of stake they'd need.
blockchain-consensus-attack-explain: Finality needs two-thirds of the stake to agree, so anyone controlling more than one-third can stall it by refusing to vote. Even then, Ethereum slowly drains the stake of validators who don't vote until finality resumes.
blockchain-consensus-slash-prompt: A validator signs two different blocks for the same turn. What happens?
blockchain-consensus-slash-fb-reward: Cheating is punished, not rewarded. Both signatures are public evidence.
blockchain-consensus-slash-opt-slashed: Part of their stake is destroyed and they're removed
blockchain-consensus-slash-fb-slashed: That's called slashing. Once anyone reports the two signatures, the network applies the punishment itself, with no judge. We'll learn more about slashing in a future lesson.
blockchain-consensus-slash-fb-nothing: Anyone can spot two conflicting signatures from the same validator and report them.
blockchain-consensus-takeaway-p1: Validators put real ETH on the line. Attacking the network means controlling a huge share of all staked ETH, and cheaters lose part of their deposit, or all of it if many cheat at once.
blockchain-nodes-summary: Switch computers off and watch the network carry on without them.
blockchain-nodes-intro-p1: Where does Ethereum actually live? Not on one company's server. It lives on thousands of computers around the world, each keeping its own copy of the blockchain.
blockchain-nodes-intro-p2: Each of those computers is a node: a computer running Ethereum software. A node downloads every new block, checks it against the rules itself and passes it on to other nodes. It doesn't take anyone's word for it, not even the validator who proposed the block.
blockchain-nodes-predict-prompt: Make a prediction: a few nodes suddenly switch off. What happens to the blockchain?
blockchain-nodes-predict-opt-stops: It stops until they come back
blockchain-nodes-predict-fb-stops: That would be true if one server ran everything. Test it in the next step.
blockchain-nodes-predict-opt-lost: The blocks stored on those nodes are lost
blockchain-nodes-predict-fb-lost: Think about how many copies of each block exist. Test it in the next step.
blockchain-nodes-predict-opt-continues: The other nodes carry on without them
blockchain-nodes-predict-fb-continues: Good instinct. Test it in the next step.
blockchain-nodes-network-prompt: Switch a node off, add a few blocks, then switch it back on.
blockchain-nodes-network-explain: The network didn't wait for the missing node. When it came back, it fetched the blocks it had missed from the other nodes and checked every one before adding it to its copy.
blockchain-nodes-sync-p1: Catching up like this is called syncing. A node that has every block up to the newest one is in sync. A node that's been offline isn't broken, just behind: it syncs when it returns, and only then can it tell you what's new.
blockchain-nodes-who-prompt: Who's allowed to run a node?
blockchain-nodes-who-fb-stake: Staking is for validators, who propose and vote on blocks. Keeping and checking a copy of the chain is a separate job.
blockchain-nodes-who-opt-approval: Only computers a company has approved
blockchain-nodes-who-fb-approval: Ethereum has no gatekeeper. The software is open source, and nobody has to sign off on who runs it.
blockchain-nodes-who-fb-anyone: Right. Ethereum is designed so a node runs on ordinary hardware, and you don't even need ETH. Validators run nodes too, with extra software and a stake on top.
blockchain-nodes-why-prompt: Your wallet shows your balance by asking a company's server. Why might you run your own node instead?
blockchain-nodes-why-opt-faster: To make the whole network faster
blockchain-nodes-why-fb-faster: One more node doesn't speed anything up. Every node still waits for the same new blocks.
blockchain-nodes-why-opt-check: To check the blockchain yourself instead of trusting someone else
blockchain-nodes-why-fb-check: Exactly. Your own node checks every block itself, so you don't have to take a server's word for what's on the chain.
blockchain-nodes-why-opt-earn: To earn rewards for checking blocks
blockchain-nodes-why-fb-earn: Rewards go to validators, who stake ETH and vote on blocks. Checking blocks on your own node doesn't pay anything.
blockchain-nodes-roles-prompt: Match each term to what it describes.
blockchain-nodes-roles-match-block: A batch of records on the chain
blockchain-nodes-roles-match-node: Keeps its own copy, no ETH needed
blockchain-nodes-roles-match-validator: Stakes ETH to propose and vote
blockchain-nodes-roles-explain: Any node keeps and checks its own copy of the chain, with no ETH required. Validators run nodes too, but they also stake ETH to propose and vote on blocks.
blockchain-nodes-takeaway-p1: Thousands of nodes each keep and check their own copy of the blockchain, so nobody is in charge and the network keeps going when some switch off.
blockchain-finality-title: Finality: when it's set in stone
blockchain-finality-summary: Checkpoints, the wait for finality and what happens to cheaters.
blockchain-finality-intro-p1: A shop sees your payment in a brand-new block. Should it hand over the goods right away? Not yet. Until a block is final, there's a small chance it gets replaced by a different one.
blockchain-finality-intro-p2: Time on Ethereum is split into 12-second slots, each a chance for one new block. Every 32 slots brings a checkpoint, so there's one about every 6.4 minutes. Validators vote on each checkpoint. Once two checkpoints in a row are each backed by validators holding two-thirds of all staked ETH, the earlier one becomes final, along with every block before it.
blockchain-finality-clock-prompt: The shop ships once your payment is final. It's in the last block before a checkpoint. Find the earliest moment it's final.
blockchain-finality-clock-explain: Validators take about 6.4 minutes to vote on each checkpoint. Once the checkpoint right after your block and the one after that are both backed by two-thirds of staked ETH, your block is final: about 13 minutes after it was added. A block added just after a checkpoint waits longer, up to about 19 minutes.
blockchain-finality-slashing-p1: What stops validators from voting to undo a final block? Breaking the rules gets a validator slashed. Signing two different blocks for the same slot, or casting votes that contradict each other, leaves signed proof. Part of its stake is destroyed and it's forced out of the network.
blockchain-finality-slashing-p2: A validator slashed on its own loses only a small part of its stake. The more staked ETH is slashed around the same time, the more each validator loses, up to all of it. So the bigger the attack, the more it costs.
blockchain-finality-offline-prompt: A validator's internet goes down for an afternoon. What happens to it?
blockchain-finality-offline-fb-slashed: Slashing is for provable cheating, like signing two conflicting blocks. Going offline isn't cheating.
blockchain-finality-offline-opt-rewards: It misses out on rewards while it's away
blockchain-finality-offline-fb-rewards: Right. While offline it earns nothing and pays a small penalty about the size of the rewards it missed, but it keeps almost all of its stake and its place.
blockchain-finality-offline-opt-waits: The network pauses until it's back
blockchain-finality-offline-fb-waits: The network never waits for one validator. Blocks keep coming without its votes.
blockchain-finality-reverse-prompt: Someone wants to undo a block that's already final. What would it take?
blockchain-finality-reverse-opt-node: Editing the copy on one node
blockchain-finality-reverse-fb-node: Other nodes check every block themselves, so an edited copy is simply rejected.
blockchain-finality-reverse-opt-majority: Getting over half of all nodes to agree
blockchain-finality-reverse-fb-majority: Finality isn't decided by counting nodes. Anyone can run as many nodes as they like.
blockchain-finality-reverse-opt-third: Validators holding at least a third of all staked ETH breaking the rules
blockchain-finality-reverse-fb-third: Right. Those rule breaks leave signed proof, so the attackers would be slashed and lose a huge amount of ETH.
blockchain-finality-recap-prompt: Fill the gaps to sum up how a block becomes final.
blockchain-finality-recap-text: Every 32 {b1} brings a new {b2}, so there's one about every 6.4 minutes. A block is {b3} once the checkpoint after it and the next one are both backed by two-thirds of staked ETH.
blockchain-finality-recap-explain: Each slot lasts 12 seconds, so 32 of them take about 6.4 minutes. A block has to wait for two checkpoints to be backed, which is why finality takes minutes, not seconds.
blockchain-finality-takeaway-p1: Normally, within about 13 to 19 minutes of being added, a block is final: undoing it would mean validators breaking the rules and getting slashed, losing a huge amount of staked ETH.
blockchain-exam-tiny-change-prompt: You hash a sentence, then add a single comma and hash it again. How do the two hashes compare?
blockchain-exam-tiny-change-opt-one: They differ by a character or two
blockchain-exam-tiny-change-opt-none: They're identical, because the meaning didn't change
blockchain-exam-tiny-change-explain: A hash function scrambles everything, so even a one-character change gives an entirely different hash. That's why a hash works as a fingerprint for spotting changed data.
blockchain-exam-work-back-prompt: A friend sends you a hash and dares you to find the message that produced it. What's your best option?
blockchain-exam-work-back-opt-reverse: Run the hash function backwards on it
blockchain-exam-work-back-opt-power: Rent time on the world's fastest computer to undo it
blockchain-exam-work-back-opt-guess: Guess messages and hash each one until one matches
blockchain-exam-work-back-explain: Hash functions only run one way, and no computer can reverse a good one. Guessing inputs and comparing their hashes is the only approach.
blockchain-exam-rewrite-prompt: Someone changes a payment recorded in block 5 of a long chain. Which blocks must they rewrite so every link matches again?
blockchain-exam-rewrite-opt-next: Only block 6, the one right after it
blockchain-exam-rewrite-opt-none: None, because the edit doesn't touch any links
blockchain-exam-rewrite-explain: Changing block 5 changes its hash, which breaks block 6's link. Fixing block 6 changes its hash in turn, so the repair has to run all the way to the newest block.
blockchain-exam-spot-edit-prompt: Why is an edited old block easy for other nodes to catch?
blockchain-exam-spot-edit-opt-report: A central company checks the chain and flags the edit
blockchain-exam-spot-edit-opt-slow: It isn't: checking hashes is so slow that edits go unnoticed for years
blockchain-exam-spot-edit-opt-links: Its hash no longer matches the link stored in the next block
blockchain-exam-spot-edit-explain: Each block stores the hash of the block before it, so an edit breaks the link that follows. Checking hashes takes a computer milliseconds, and every node checks the blocks it receives.
blockchain-exam-stall-prompt: An attacker wants to stop blocks from becoming final by refusing to vote. What's the smallest share of all staked ETH they'd need?
blockchain-exam-stall-explain: A block becomes final only once validators holding two-thirds of all staked ETH agree. Anyone holding more than a third can keep that from happening by not voting.
blockchain-exam-double-sign-prompt: A validator signs two different blocks for the same slot. What happens to it?
blockchain-exam-double-sign-opt-penalty: It pays a small penalty about the size of one missed reward and carries on
blockchain-exam-double-sign-opt-slashed: It loses part of its stake and is removed from validating
blockchain-exam-double-sign-opt-nothing: Nothing, since nobody can tell which block it meant
blockchain-exam-double-sign-explain: Two conflicting signatures are public proof of cheating, so the validator is slashed. Small penalties are for going offline, which isn't cheating.
blockchain-exam-back-online-prompt: Your node is switched off for a day while the network keeps adding blocks. What happens when you switch it back on?
blockchain-exam-back-online-opt-broken: It's broken and has to start again from an empty copy
blockchain-exam-back-online-opt-trust: It adds the missed blocks without checking them, since other nodes already did
blockchain-exam-back-online-opt-sync: It fetches the blocks it missed from other nodes, checks each one and catches up
blockchain-exam-back-online-explain: Catching up like this is called syncing. An offline node is just behind, not broken, and it checks every missed block itself before adding it to its copy.
blockchain-exam-run-node-prompt: Which of these are true about running your own node?
blockchain-exam-run-node-opt-anyone: Anyone can run one on an ordinary computer
blockchain-exam-run-node-opt-stake: You have to stake ETH first
blockchain-exam-run-node-opt-check: It lets you check the blockchain yourself instead of trusting someone else's server
blockchain-exam-run-node-opt-earn: It earns rewards for every block it checks
blockchain-exam-run-node-explain: A node runs on ordinary hardware with no stake or permission needed, and it checks every block itself. Staking and rewards belong to validators, which is a separate job.
blockchain-exam-wait-prompt: A shop waits until your payment is final before shipping. Roughly how long after your payment's block is added will that take?
blockchain-exam-wait-opt-block: About 12 seconds, once the next block arrives
blockchain-exam-wait-opt-thirteen: About 13 to 19 minutes, once two checkpoints in a row are backed
blockchain-exam-wait-opt-checkpoint: About 6.4 minutes, once the next checkpoint is backed
blockchain-exam-wait-explain: A checkpoint comes every 32 slots, about every 6.4 minutes. Your block is final once the two checkpoints after it are each backed by validators holding two-thirds of staked ETH, 13 to 19 minutes after it was added, depending on how close to a checkpoint it landed.
blockchain-exam-undo-prompt: An exchange credited your deposit once its block was final. Someone wants to erase that block. What would it take?
blockchain-exam-undo-opt-third: Validators with a third or more of all staked ETH breaking the rules
blockchain-exam-undo-opt-edit: Editing the block on their own node
blockchain-exam-undo-opt-nodes: Running more than half of all the nodes
blockchain-exam-undo-explain: Finality depends on staked ETH, not on counting nodes, and an edited copy is simply rejected. Breaking the rules leaves signed proof, so those validators would be slashed, and the more staked ETH is slashed at once, the more each one loses.
